summary: Generative AI apps and autonomous agents introduce risks classic security controls don't see: a model can be tricked into leaking data (prompt injection/jailbreak), it can surface data a user is technically allowed to open but shouldn't see (oversharing/overexposure), and agents act with their own identity to take real actions. SC-500 splits AI security into three layers — **data** (Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI), **identity** (Microsoft Entra Agent ID), and **threat/posture** (Microsoft Defender for AI Services plus Microsoft Foundry guardrails and an AI gateway in front of model endpoints). Each layer answers a different question: what sensitive data can the AI touch, who is the agent and can Conditional Access govern it, and what threats/misconfigurations put the deployment itself at risk.
keyPoints: **Purview DSPM for AI** discovers **oversharing before Copilot amplifies it**: run a data risk assessment against high-risk SharePoint sites to find overly broad sharing (e.g. "everyone except external", anonymous links) — because Copilot can expose any content a user is technically permitted to open.

DSPM for AI **one-click policies** cover three jobs: capture Copilot prompts/responses, detect sensitive information pasted into AI sites, and detect risky AI usage; results surface in **Reports** and **Activity explorer ▸ AI activities**. Requires Audit enabled, the Purview browser extension, device onboarding, and a **Purview/Microsoft 365 E5** license.

**Microsoft Entra Agent ID** extends Entra identity to AI agents (the identity foundation of **Microsoft Agent 365**): every agent built in Foundry or Copilot Studio gets a governed **agent identity** so Conditional Access, Identity Protection risk, and governance apply to it like a human user.

Key agent-identity concepts: **agent identity** (the non-human identity the agent authenticates and acts as), **agent's user account** (a linked account with its own mailbox/groups, for "digital colleague" scenarios), **agent identity blueprint** (a template that creates agent identities consistently — the blueprint itself cannot access resources), and **custom security attributes** (business labels, e.g. `AgentApprovalStatus=IT_Approved`, that Conditional Access policies can target).

**Conditional Access for agents**: create a policy targeting the **Agents (Preview)** assignment (all agent identities, or scoped by custom security attribute), condition **Agent risk (Preview) = High**, grant control **Block access** — roll out in **Report-only** first, then enforce.

**Scope trap**: CA on an agent identity protects the agent's **token**, not its linked user account — these are separate scopes to configure independently. CA also only governs resources secured by Entra ID; an agent calling an API with a **raw API key bypasses Entra entirely**, so CA never applies — use Entra-based auth instead of API keys.

Once Entra flags an agent as high-risk, use **Defender XDR** to assess its **blast radius** (which resources/data/identities it could reach), contain it (block/revoke access), and right-size its permissions; manage the ongoing access lifecycle (review/approve/remove) via **Entra ID Governance** and **Agent 365**.

**Microsoft Defender for AI Services** (a Defender for Cloud plan) watches Microsoft Foundry/Azure OpenAI and alerts on jailbreak/prompt injection (via **Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields**), data leakage, **ASCII-smuggling** indirect injection, credential theft, and **wallet attacks** (cost abuse) — alerts surface in Defender XDR. Enable it in **Defender for Cloud ▸ Environment settings ▸ Defender plans**, then turn on **user prompt evidence** and, if Purview-licensed, data security for AI interactions.

**Microsoft Foundry guardrails** apply to model input and output: **content filters** (severity thresholds for hate/violence/sexual/self-harm), **Prompt Shields** (blocks direct jailbreaks and indirect/document injection), **blocklists** (custom banned terms), and protected-material/groundedness checks. For agents, also enable a jailbreak control, an indirect prompt injection control, and an **MCP allowed-tools list** so the agent can only invoke approved tools.

**AI gateway via Azure API Management**: placing APIM in front of model endpoints enforces **Entra ID authentication instead of API keys**, applies **token-based rate-limiting/quotas** (defends against wallet attacks), load-balances across deployments, and centralizes logging to Azure Monitor — without changing the app.

**Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps** provides **real-time runtime protection specifically for Copilot Studio agents** — distinct from Defender for AI Services (which watches Foundry/Azure OpenAI). Enable it under the Defender portal's **Settings ▸ AI**, then coordinate with **Power Platform admins** to configure the correct **App ID** so the agent is recognized; only then does agent inventory, alerts, and Advanced Hunting data appear correctly in Microsoft Defender XDR.

**Microsoft Agent 365** is the **management and governance plane** for AI agents deployed across the Microsoft 365 environment — distinct from Entra Agent ID, which is the underlying **identity layer** an agent authenticates with. Through Agent 365 you enable the management interface, **register agents**, apply access controls, and **monitor agent activity/usage** to enforce organizational AI governance policies over the agent's full lifecycle.

**Defender for Cloud's AI workloads plan** bundles **CSPM** (posture: misconfigurations, oversharing risk signals) and **CWP** (Defender for AI Services runtime alerts) for AI resources specifically, behind a single enablement toggle; results and combined insights surface in the **Data and AI security dashboard**, which correlates posture and threat findings for AI workloads in one place.

Agents deployed to Microsoft 365 are governed from the **Microsoft 365 admin center**, which is the management plane for the agent fleet: which agents exist, who may use them, and whether an agent is approved for the tenant. **Microsoft Entra Agent ID** supplies each agent's identity, and **Agent 365** is the layer that registers, approves and monitors deployed agents — identity and management are separate concerns and both are needed.

The tenant-level lever worth knowing is **which agents users may install or invoke at all**: an agent nobody approved should not be reachable, and that decision lives with the Microsoft 365 admin rather than with the agent author. Combine it with a **custom security attribute** (for example `AgentApprovalStatus=IT_Approved`) so one Conditional Access policy covers every approved agent automatically instead of naming them one by one.
commonPitfalls: Confusing **Purview DSPM for AI** (data-centric: which sensitive data agents/Copilot touch, oversharing, DLP for AI sites, needs a Purview/M365 E5 license) with **Defender for AI Services** (threat detection on Foundry/Azure OpenAI, configured as a Defender for Cloud plan) — different products, different licenses, different questions answered.
Assuming a Conditional Access policy scoped to "agents" also covers the **agent's linked user account** — they are separate assignment scopes; both must be configured if both paths need protection.

Believing Conditional Access protects every agent action — it only governs resources secured by **Entra ID**. An agent invoking an API with a **raw API key** bypasses Entra and CA entirely, which is exactly why Entra-based auth is recommended over API keys.
Enabling Microsoft 365 Copilot tenant-wide **before** running a DSPM for AI data risk assessment — by the time oversharing is found, Copilot may already have surfaced it to the wrong users.

Treating **content filters** and **Prompt Shields** as the same Foundry control — content filters catch harmful content categories, while Prompt Shields specifically target jailbreak and (in)direct prompt injection attempts.
Leaving an agent without an **MCP allowed-tools list** — an unrestricted agent can invoke arbitrary tools/data sources, which massively widens the blast radius if the agent is later compromised.

Confusing **Microsoft Agent 365** (the governance/lifecycle plane — register, approve, monitor usage of deployed agents) with **Microsoft Entra Agent ID** (the underlying non-human identity an agent authenticates with) — Agent 365 governs agents *using* the identity Entra Agent ID provides; it doesn't replace it.

Assuming Copilot Studio agent protection in Defender for Cloud Apps is automatic once toggled on — without also configuring the agent's **App ID** with Power Platform admins, agent inventory and alerts stay incomplete in Defender XDR even though the setting shows as enabled.

Assuming that provisioning an **Entra Agent ID** is the whole of agent governance — the identity makes the agent addressable by policy, whereas approving it, publishing it to users and monitoring its usage happen in the Microsoft 365 admin center and Agent 365.

Governing agents by naming them individually in Conditional Access: the list is out of date the moment an agent is added. Target a **custom security attribute** instead, so approval and policy scope stay in step.

summary: VM disk encryption stacks three optional layers on top of always-on platform encryption, chosen by requirement rather than by "more is better": **encryption at host**, **Azure Disk Encryption (ADE)**, and **server-side encryption with a customer-managed key (CMK)**. **Azure Bastion** and **Just-In-Time (JIT) VM access** are complementary controls that together eliminate standing exposure of management ports. **Defender for Servers Plan 2** adds vulnerability scanning, file integrity monitoring, and **agentless scanning** on top of Plan 1's EDR, and **Azure Arc** is the bridge that lets non-Azure servers receive the same governance and protection.
keyPoints: **Encryption at host** encrypts a VM's temp and cache disks **at the host level**, with **no in-guest agent** — the modern recommended default for coverage that ADE alone doesn't provide.

**Azure Disk Encryption (ADE)** encrypts **inside the guest OS** using BitLocker (Windows) or dm-crypt (Linux), with keys stored in **Key Vault** — use it when OS-level volume encryption is a specific requirement.
**Server-side encryption with a customer-managed key (CMK)** is platform-managed disk encryption where you supply the key via a **disk encryption set** — no in-guest component at all.
**Azure Bastion**: browser/portal-based RDP/SSH over **TLS** — the VM needs **no public IP** and never has 3389/22 exposed to the internet.

**Just-In-Time (JIT) VM access** (a Defender for Cloud workload-protection feature): management ports stay **closed by default**; an approved, time- and source-IP-scoped request opens them temporarily via NSG/Firewall rules, then closes them again.

**Trusted launch** adds **Secure Boot + vTPM + boot integrity monitoring** to a VM's security type, defending against rootkits/boot-kits; **confidential VMs** go further and add hardware-based **memory encryption (TEE)**.
**Azure Machine Configuration** (formerly Guest Configuration) audits or enforces in-guest settings — e.g. password policy, installed applications — via **Azure Policy**.

**Defender for Servers Plan 1** = Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (**MDE/EDR**) only. **Plan 2** = everything: EDR, vulnerability scanning (**MDVM**), agentless malware/secret scanning, file integrity monitoring, JIT, adaptive application controls, plus 500 GB/day of free data ingestion.

**Azure Arc** projects on-premises and other-cloud servers (and Kubernetes, SQL, etc.) into Azure as Arc-enabled resources, so Azure Policy, RBAC, Defender for Cloud, and Machine Configuration apply as if they were native Azure resources — the bridge for hybrid and multicloud security.

**Agentless scanning** (Defender for Servers Plan 2) safely snapshots a VM's disk and analyzes it out-of-band to find vulnerabilities, malware, and exposed secrets **without installing an agent** or affecting VM performance — it complements, but doesn't fully replace, agent-based MDE.
commonPitfalls: **Bastion and JIT combine — they are not alternatives**: Bastion removes the need for a public IP/exposed RDP-SSH; JIT keeps management ports closed until an explicit approved request. Use both together for the strongest posture.

Choosing a disk-encryption layer by "more is better" instead of by requirement: **ADE** for in-guest BitLocker/dm-crypt, **encryption at host** for temp/cache coverage without an agent, **CMK** when platform-level customer key control is the ask.
Assuming **Defender for Servers Plan 1** includes vulnerability scanning, agentless scanning, or JIT — those are **Plan 2 only**; Plan 1 is EDR (MDE) alone.
Forgetting that non-Azure servers must be **Azure Arc-onboarded** before Azure Policy, RBAC, or Defender for Cloud can manage or protect them.
Treating **agentless scanning** as a replacement for MDE — it's a complementary, point-in-time snapshot analysis, not real-time endpoint detection and response.
Confusing **Trusted launch** (Secure Boot + vTPM + integrity monitoring) with **confidential VMs** (adds hardware-based memory encryption) — they are different, stackable security tiers.

commands.task: Create a VM with encryption at host enabled (covers temp/cache disks, no in-guest agent)
commands.cli: az vm create --name VM1 --resource-group RG1 --image Ubuntu2204 --encryption-at-host true

commands.task: Enable Azure Disk Encryption on a VM, keys stored in Key Vault
commands.cli: az vm encryption enable --name VM1 --resource-group RG1 --disk-encryption-keyvault KV1

commands.task: Create a Trusted launch VM (Secure Boot + vTPM)
commands.cli: az vm create --name VM1 --resource-group RG1 --image Ubuntu2204 --security-type TrustedLaunch --enable-secure-boot true --enable-vtpm true

summary: **Microsoft Defender for Containers** covers image scanning and runtime threat detection across AKS, Arc-enabled clusters, and other clouds, while **AKS** and **ACR** each need their own identity, network, and admission hardening. **App Service**, **Functions**, and **Logic Apps** share a common security pattern — built-in auth, network restriction, and managed identity — while a **Web Application Firewall** and **API Management** protect the web and API layers respectively, each at the right scope: regional versus global, exploit-blocking versus auth/throttling.
keyPoints: **Microsoft Defender for Containers** finds misconfigurations and runtime risk across Kubernetes: **image vulnerability scanning** (in ACR and at runtime), runtime threat detection, and hardening recommendations — covers AKS, **Arc-enabled clusters**, and other clouds (EKS/GKE).

**AKS hardening**: Microsoft Entra integration with **Kubernetes RBAC**, **private clusters** (no public API server endpoint), Kubernetes **network policies** (pod-to-pod traffic control), **Azure Policy for AKS** (Gatekeeper admission control), **workload identity**, and pulling secrets from Key Vault via the **CSI driver**.

**ACR hardening**: **disable the admin user** (shared, non-attributable credential), use **Entra/RBAC and repository-scoped tokens** instead, add a **private endpoint**, enable **content trust** (image signing), and use **quarantine + vulnerability scanning** for pushed images.
**ACI/Container Apps**: deploy into a **VNet**, use **managed identity** for registry pulls instead of credentials, and restrict ingress.

**App Service**: built-in authentication (**Easy Auth**) with Entra, **HTTPS-only + minimum TLS version**, access restrictions/IP rules, VNet integration & private endpoints, and **managed identity** to reach Key Vault/SQL without stored secrets.

**Azure Functions**: Entra authentication, function/host **keys** for HTTP triggers, network restrictions, private endpoints, and managed identity — the same pattern as App Service, adapted to triggers.
**Logic Apps**: managed identity, IP access control, secure parameters stored in **Key Vault**, and private connectivity via **ISE or Standard plan inside a VNet**.

**Web Application Firewall (WAF)**: applies the **OWASP Core Rule Set** on **Application Gateway** (regional) or **Front Door** (global) — blocks SQLi/XSS, supports custom rules and bot/rate-limit rules; **Prevention mode blocks**, **Detection mode only logs**.

**Azure API Management (APIM)** protects back-end APIs: **subscription keys**, Entra/OAuth (JWT) validation, IP filtering, and **rate-limit/quota policies**, and can expose APIs **privately** rather than the raw backend.

**WAF placement rule**: use **Application Gateway WAF** for a regional app that needs path-based routing inside a VNet; use **Front Door WAF** for a global, internet-facing app that needs CDN/edge presence and anycast. WAF blocks web exploits; APIM protects the API layer (auth, throttling) — commonly used together.

**Azure Container Instances (ACI)** and **Azure Container Apps** are secured like any other Azure-hosted workload, with three controls doing the work: deploy into a **VNet** (or a Container Apps environment bound to one) so the container is not reachable from the internet; use a **managed identity** for registry pulls and for downstream access, so no registry password lives in a deployment template; and pull from a **private-endpoint-only ACR** with the admin account disabled.

Ingress is the setting that most often stays too open: Container Apps ingress can be **internal** (VNet-only) or **external**, and ACI exposes a public IP unless it is deployed into a subnet. Restricting ingress is a separate decision from securing the pull — a container with a credential-free pull and public ingress is still publicly reachable.
commonPitfalls: Underestimating **Defender for Containers**' scope — it covers image scanning **and** runtime detection across AKS, Arc-enabled clusters, and other clouds, not just AKS-native workloads.
Forgetting to **disable the ACR admin account** — it's a shared, non-attributable credential and one of the most tested hardening steps for registries.

Choosing **Application Gateway** when the scenario needs a **global**, internet-facing app with CDN/edge and anycast — that calls for **Front Door**; App Gateway is regional, VNet-scoped, path-based routing.

Treating **WAF** and **APIM** as interchangeable — WAF blocks web exploits (SQLi/XSS); APIM protects the API layer (authentication, throttling). They complement each other, they don't replace one another.
Leaving a WAF policy in **Detection mode** and assuming attacks are blocked — Detection only **logs** matches; **Prevention** is required to actually stop them.
Assuming Kubernetes **network policies** alone secure an AKS cluster — they only govern pod-to-pod traffic; private cluster, Entra/RBAC, and workload identity cover the other layers.

Passing registry credentials to ACI in the deployment command (`--registry-password`) because it is the documented quick start — that puts the registry password into the template, the pipeline log and the resource definition. A managed identity with **AcrPull** removes all three copies.
Leaving **external ingress** on a Container App that only serves internal callers: the app is then on the public internet, whatever the network configuration of the containers behind it.

commands.task: Create an AKS cluster with Entra integration, Azure RBAC for Kubernetes, and a private API server
Disable the shared admin account on Azure Container Registry
Enable the Defender for Containers plan on a subscription
commands.cli: az security pricing create --name Containers --tier Standard

commands.task: Create a WAF policy on Application Gateway in Prevention mode with the OWASP rule set
commands.cli:
az network application-gateway waf-policy create --name waf1 --resource-group RG1
az network application-gateway waf-policy policy-setting update --policy-name waf1 --resource-group RG1 --mode Prevention
commands.powershell:
New-AzApplicationGatewayFirewallPolicy -Name waf1 -ResourceGroupName RG1
Set-AzApplicationGatewayFirewallPolicySetting -Name waf1 -ResourceGroupName RG1 -Mode Prevention

commands.task: Create a container instance in a VNet subnet, pulling from ACR with a managed identity instead of a registry password
commands.cli: az container create --name app1 --resource-group RG1 --image acr1.azurecr.io/app:1.0 --vnet VNet1 --subnet aci-subnet --assign-identity <userAssignedIdentityId> --acr-identity <userAssignedIdentityId>
